name: Garlic-Ginger Chicken Breasts with Cilantro and Mint
headnote: The author credits this to an aunt, Sonia, who guarded the marinade recipe from the rest of the family for years and would vanish for half an hour on vacations to mix it in secret. After much coaxing the formula was finally handed over. Both the marinade and the low, slowish cooking method are presented as the key ideas; the result is charred, spicy and juicy, good plain or wrapped in a roti.
comment_digest: The highest-voted thread (819 votes) is not about cooking at all but a complaint about the recipe calling for a disposable zip-top bag to marinate in; a 465-vote reply gives the practical alternative, marinating in a bowl just large enough to hold chicken plus marinade and massaging it in by hand, which is how Indian cooks did it before plastic. Several others (189, 154 votes) counter that zip bags wash and reuse fine. A 449-vote comment reports making it as written with excellent results and pushes back on the derailment. One popular note supplies a raita to serve alongside: yogurt, seeded chopped English cucumber, cilantro, green onion and ground spice. Little disagreement on technique itself.
flags: top comments dominated by an off-topic plastic-bag debate rather than cooking notes

name: Gateau Reine De Saba
headnote: Nigella Lawson offers her own simplified take on the cake Julia Child described as the first French cake she ever ate. She melts the chocolate with liquid and uses all ground almonds instead of the usual almond-and-flour mix, which also makes it gluten-free. She wants the texture closer to pudding, dense and melting, and notes a small slice goes a long way, so one cake serves about twelve.
comment_digest: The most-voted note (81) argues a plain ganache of chocolate and cream beats the recipe's glaze and skips corn syrup entirely; a 30-vote reply defends the corn syrup as what keeps the glaze glossy and suggests keeping a small bottle just for glazing. Another popular commenter substituted raw honey for the corn syrup successfully. On the almonds, a 46-vote note clarifies that ground almonds and almond flour are essentially the same thing, ground almonds simply being the British term, and a baker reports good results with roughly 1 1/4 cups almond flour plus 1/2 cup almond meal. One person's cake rose higher and domed more than the photograph but was still well received. Several non-US readers grumble about butter measured in tablespoons.

name: Greek Baked Fish with Tomatoes and Onions
headnote: Martha Rose Shulman frames this as the baked fish you meet travelling in the Greek islands, a robust tomato-and-onion sauce that needs a firm white fish under it. She points readers to the Monterey Bay Aquarium's sustainability rankings and suggests Pacific cod, halibut, black cod or striped bass, with US mahi mahi as a second-tier choice. It ran with a piece on healthier fish dishes.
comment_digest: The strongest practical correction (52 votes) is on timing: cooks say it takes nowhere near the stated two hours, that the first step is unnecessary, and that the fish is done in as little as 20 minutes. On seasoning, a 62-vote note would drop the tomato paste, which makes the sauce heavy, and use tomatoes alone plus a little red pepper. Several skip the sugar without missing it. Popular additions are red bell pepper and pitted olives (37 votes), while a commenter from a Greek village family says raisins, allspice and cinnamon belong in it and cod is the fish of choice there (35). Another suggests swapping the fish for a couple of cans of chickpeas for a vegetarian version. An 84-vote note simply confirms it works exactly as written.

name: Greek Lemon Potatoes
headnote: A classic Greek approach to roast potatoes: peel them and roast in equal parts olive oil, lemon juice and chicken stock so the interiors stay creamy while the high oven heat crisps the outsides. The potatoes drink up the seasoned liquid as they cook. Russets can be used the same way but come out drier than the recommended potato.
comment_digest: This one splits sharply. The single most-voted comment (2,175) is a joke at the recipe's expense, renaming it after burnt potatoes and ruined sheet pans, and a 1,041-vote note goes further: skip the stock altogether, just toss the potatoes with lemon juice, oil and seasonings and roast on a sheet pan. Against that, a 1,508-vote comment insists the stock is essential, makes it exactly as written, and notes vegetable stock works for a vegan version. The most useful technique tips are to marinate the potatoes in the liquid for a few hours before baking so the lemon penetrates (832 votes), and to toss everything in a bowl before transferring to the pan, with a tablespoon of flour added for extra crispness (626).
flags: strong disagreement in comments over whether the stock helps or causes scorching

name: Grilled or Oven-Roasted Santa Maria Tri-Tip
headnote: Sourcing is the first hurdle: you may have to ask a butcher or the store's meat manager to order a tri-tip, and two pounds is the useful size, though a bigger one yields sandwich leftovers. The headnote's main technical point is carving, since the grain changes direction within this cut. Inspect the raw roast to see where the muscle fibres shift, and after a 15-minute rest cut the roast in two at that junction and slice each half separately against its own grain.
comment_digest: The most-voted note (380) calls tri-tip the best underused cut and reassures cooks that the rub survives missing ingredients. The main methodological split is oven versus grill: a 344-vote commenter uses a dry rub, wraps in foil and holds it at 250F for about three hours, while a 225-vote cook browns the fat side over direct heat then moves to indirect at high temperature for 10 to 15 minutes, using the oven only in bad weather. Regional authenticity draws sharp comment: a fifth-generation Santa Maria native (193 votes) says the real meal is tri-tip with pinquito beans, green salad, garlic-buttered French bread and salsa, and flags the coffee in this rub as a departure from tradition. Another (116) wants the Times to report the original barbecue properly.

name: Italian Fennel Sausage
headnote: Samin Nosrat's homemade bulk sausage scented with fennel, meant for pasta, pizza, Thanksgiving stuffing, soup, or fried as patties with crusty bread and olive-oil-soaked white beans. Her one insistence is fat content: ground pork at roughly 20 percent fat by weight, and 25 percent does no harm. If only lean pork is available, she suggests having the butcher swap a couple of ounces of it for ground pork belly or bacon.
comment_digest: With only sixteen comments the discussion is small but converges on one issue: salt. The top note (27 votes) explains the recipe assumes Diamond Crystal kosher, and that Morton kosher should be cut to 1.5 teaspoons and table salt to 1 teaspoon. A cook who used Morton's at the full 2 teaspoons confirms it came out too salty (16 votes), and another simply says to halve the salt next time. On substitutions, turkey and grass-fed beef both worked for people avoiding pork, though one commenter asks pointedly whether the turkey version had fat added. A 9-vote note suggests grinding your own pork butt or stew meat and freely adding garlic and onion powder, paprika, thyme, oregano or marjoram, and anise in place of some fennel. One tip: shape patties in a cheap circular cookie mold, filled halfway so they are not too thick.

name: Italian Lemon-Ricotta Cake
headnote: A very short headnote: this is migliaccio, a Carnival-season lemon and ricotta cheesecake from Italy. What sets it apart from a standard cheesecake is a base built on semolina flour, which gives it a noticeably lighter texture.
comment_digest: The loudest complaint (235 votes) is the pan size: the recipe calls for an 11-inch cake pan that few home cooks own, and commenters report a 10-inch pan works with slightly longer baking. The second theme is lemon intensity, with repeated votes for more than the recipe specifies. One cook used the zest of three lemons in a 10-inch springform to great success at a dinner party (110), another added the zest of two large lemons plus a tablespoon of fresh juice for a more lemony batter (91), and a third went to four lemons' zest and still found the result only good rather than outstanding (63). A pizzeria owner (145 votes) shares a Naples-inspired version tuned over months using fine semolina. One cook suggests using leftover whey from homemade ricotta in the batter. Several appreciate that the cake is crustless.

name: Julia Child's Berry Clafoutis
headnote: Julia Moskin presents this as a quietly elegant dessert that is far easier than it looks, easy enough to assemble while the main course finishes in the oven. Fresh berries matter, and it should go to the table warm. Blueberries or blackberries are specified but the batter takes whatever fruit is in season.
comment_digest: Two arguments dominate. The first is what to call it: a 376-vote note says this is clafoutis rather than flan and warns that clafoutis often turns out too eggy and custardy, fixable with a little baking powder; a 263-vote comment doubts the Julia Child attribution altogether, pointing out that a recipe permitting 2 percent milk is not hers, and others agree it sits somewhere between flan and clafoutis. The second is whether the criticism is fair: a 630-vote comment says the negative notes are overblown, the recipe works as written, and reducing sugar is fine if you prefer. The single most-voted comment (751) simply supplies a rival apricot-and-almond clafoutis from Richard Olney. A 736-vote note reports it looks dull but silenced the table once served slightly cooled in small dishes.
flags: comments dispute both the name and the Julia Child attribution

name: Leek and Potato Soup
headnote: No headnote text is published for this one. The page carries only a credit line placing it in Pierre Franey's 60-Minute Gourmet column.
comment_digest: The dominant thread is a genuine error in the published method: the recipe never says when to add the potatoes. The top comment (106 votes) guesses they go in with the chicken broth and water, and a 76-vote reply quotes the newspaper's own correction from December 25, 1991, which restored the omitted step to the 60-Minute Gourmet version printed a week earlier. A third commenter (29 votes) is exasperated that the omission persists years after being flagged, and asks whether the potatoes should be sauteed with the leeks or simply dropped into the liquid. Beyond that the notes are warm and brief: a 23-vote comment calls it the simplest leek-potato soup and the best. Practical tweaks include using mostly olive oil with a little butter for flavour, adding leftover ham and croutons, using extra potato, and substituting four smaller leeks when large ones are unavailable. Several note it is not pureed and are surprised how good that is.
flags: no headnote published; recipe as printed omits the step for adding the potatoes, per a 1991 NYT correction quoted in comments

name: Leek Risotto with Sugar Snap Peas and Pancetta
headnote: The headnote is mostly a risotto technique lesson: constant stirring is a myth, but the dish still needs watching. Keep the rice lightly coated in liquid and bubbling briskly, and add more stock only just before the grains threaten to catch on the pan bottom. Stir harder and more often in the second half of cooking, once the starch starts coming out, for the creamiest texture.
comment_digest: The busiest thread is a rice argument. The top note (120 votes) objects that NYT risotto recipes always call for arborio and argues it is the wrong choice for a creamy result, implicitly favouring carnaroli or vialone nano. A 56-vote reply dismisses the whole debate as precious, pointing out it is all short-grain rice, and a 17-vote comment calls the fussiness elitist given pandemic-era shortages, reporting that sushi rice worked when nothing else was on the shelf. The most useful cooking tip (20 votes) is to blanch the sugar snaps for one minute and slice them crosswise rather than lengthwise, which keeps them green and crunchy without tasting raw, plus a recommendation to make extra bacon or pancetta. One cook folded in diced butternut squash successfully.

name: Leek, Mushroom and Goat Cheese Tart
headnote: A savoury tart assembled on store-bought puff pastry and topped with goat cheese, fennel, mushrooms and leeks. It is pitched two ways: as an easy but impressive appetizer for a party, or as a weeknight dinner for two. It ran with a menu piece about cooking for guests without missing the party.
comment_digest: The most-voted note (65) says the tart needs a flavour boost and recommends herbed goat cheese, thyme and rosemary with the vegetables, and a balsamic drizzle; a separate commenter endorses about a tablespoon of fresh thyme added to the mushrooms. Technique: saute the mushrooms in batches so they brown rather than steam (35 votes), and pie crust works in place of puff pastry. On making it ahead, a 30-vote reply is firm that assembling early gives a soggy result, but you can bake the crust and cook the vegetables through step three in advance and hold them. A recurring confusion (23 votes) is why the pastry is halved, with cooks unsure whether it makes two tarts or stacked layers. One cook substituted feta for goat cheese and was disappointed, suspecting that was the problem. Flatbread also works as a base.
flags: several commenters confused by the instruction to cut the puff pastry in half

name: Lemon Bars with Olive Oil and Sea Salt
headnote: Melissa Clark's grown-up version of the childhood lemon bar, keeping the shortbread base and tart curd but adding the bitterness of good olive oil and a scatter of sea salt on top for a faintly savoury edge. She stresses that the oil must have character, ideally herbal and fresh with a peppery finish, or the whole point is lost. They keep up to five days refrigerated but taste brightest within a day of baking.
comment_digest: A runny curd is the problem cooks hit, and the highest-voted technical notes address it directly. An 864-vote comment says the curd either never reached a vigorous enough boil or was boiled too long, and a 574-vote follow-up reports solving it by holding the boil for close to the full minute rather than cutting it short. A 431-vote comment recommends replacing the cornstarch with potato starch, which stands up better to heat and acidity and does not weep the way cornstarch does. A 1,008-vote comment praises the recipe for giving gram weights and urges the Times to do it everywhere, though it flags an issue with the format. The single most-voted note (1,332) is a delighted ten-year-old baker reporting success. Several cooks now make them repeatedly on request.

name: Lemony Shrimp and Bean Stew
headnote: Ali Slagle's weeknight stew needs little prep and cooks fast but reads as more elegant than the effort suggests. The headnote offers several routes: swap the shrimp for an equal weight of flaky white fish or seared scallops, or stretch it to serve six by stirring in butter and spooning it over spaghetti or rigatoni. A generous pour of good olive oil at the end is encouraged.
comment_digest: The single most-voted comment (3,145) answers a make-ahead question and warns that shrimp reheated after cooking goes rubbery and flavourless; the fix is to mix the marinade without the shrimp, make the leek and bean base ahead, and add the shrimp only when reheating to serve. The second-biggest tip (2,196 votes) is to build a quick stock from the shrimp shells instead of using chicken stock, sauteing the shells in a little oil for about three minutes, deglazing with a quarter cup of dry white wine and simmering. Balance adjustments recur: less shrimp, more beans and more broth (741 votes). Shallots substitute for leeks and a bag of spinach adds greens. A 2,006-vote note reports making it exactly as written with no changes at all.

name: Lisbon Chocolate Cake
headnote: Dorie Greenspan tells the story behind it: pickpocketed of all her credit cards on Lisbon's No. 28 tram on her first day, she nearly left the city, but she and her husband Michael worked through their eating list anyway and found this cake at Landeau Chocolate on the last day. Her version is a dense but not heavy brownie-like base under a whipped chocolate ganache with the texture of mousse, finished with a heavy dusting of cocoa. Since the cake is nothing but chocolate, she says to use one you genuinely like.
comment_digest: A former pastry chef's note leads at 837 votes, recommending Valrhona cocoa for assertive chocolate flavour without bitterness and good colour. The most repeated practical change is baking in a springform pan (757 and 441 votes), which removes the awkward transfer; one cook also spread a layer of ganache on the serving plate before setting the cake down. A pinch of espresso powder in the batter is a popular addition, and several report the mousse set without trouble when made a day ahead. A 311-vote comment flags that the cake is flourless and therefore gluten-free. A large tangent (755 and 653 votes) debates whether preheating the oven first is wasteful, with the reply explaining that oven thermostats sense one corner and the cavity needs longer to even out than the beep suggests.

name: Maple Pear Upside-Down Cake
headnote: No headnote is published; the page carries only the credit placing it in a Times column on upside-down pear cake.
comment_digest: Sweetness of the maple topping is the recurring complaint and the main disagreement. A 48-vote note says the topping comes out soupy and too sweet while the cake itself works as advertised, proposing to cut the maple syrup to about half a cup and reduce the brown sugar. A 77-vote comment simply omits the brown sugar on a repeat bake, and a 47-vote cook did the same and reports it turned out perfectly with a clean flip and no sogginess. Pushing back, a 33-vote commenter says ignore the reviews claiming three-quarters of a cup of syrup is too much and notes cooling the cake closer to 15 minutes before inverting. A 75-vote note recommends reducing the caramel longer than the recipe says. One commenter supplies a vegan adaptation using two tablespoons of ground flaxseed with six tablespoons of warm water in place of the eggs.

name: Marcella Hazan’s Bolognese Sauce
headnote: After Marcella Hazan died in 2013 the Times asked readers which of her recipes had entered their regular rotation, and the answer that came back most often was her Bolognese. She wrote several versions; this is the one from Essentials of Classic Italian Cooking, which one reader called the gold standard.
comment_digest: With over 3,000 notes the top-voted entry (11,324) is a much-loved anecdote about a Labrador eating the cooling sauce rather than cooking advice. The substantive guidance sits just below. A 4,747-vote question asks whether the separated fat should be skimmed at the end, which is the step newcomers find unclear. A cook of 25 years (2,362 votes) confirms it works with all beef or a beef, pork and veal mix. A 2,076-vote comment insists that disappointing results come from deviating and urges following Hazan exactly, particularly the slow simmer. Importantly, a 1,923-vote commenter working from the 1979 edition reports materially different proportions there, giving three tablespoons each of olive oil and butter for three-quarters of a pound of beef, so the published ratios are not the only authoritative ones.
flags: commenters report the 1979 edition of the book gives different ingredient proportions

name: Mark Furstenberg's White Bread
headnote: A short note from the Washington Post crediting baker Mark Furstenberg, who specifies a bread flour of roughly 12 percent protein for this loaf. Storage advice is to keep the loaf unwrapped, cut side down on a board, and eat it within three days. The recipe builds on a small white sponge or starter and is already given in grams alongside cup measures, making about a pound and a half of bread.
comment_digest: NO COMMENTS
flags: Washington Post page; reviews section shows zero comments, rating based on only 2 ratings; recipe already published with gram weights

name: Meatballs with Any Meat
headnote: Melissa Clark presents this as a ratio to memorise rather than a fixed recipe: one pound of any ground meat, half a cup of breadcrumbs for lightness, a teaspoon of salt and one egg to bind. Everything else, pepper and spices, chopped herbs, minced garlic, onion, scallion or shallot, is adjustable, and even fish works. Broil or fry as you prefer. The page notes she tested at least half a dozen approaches before a professional tester repeated the recipe a minimum of three times.
comment_digest: Cooking method divides the comments. The top note (1,273 votes) borrows an Alton Brown approach, rolling the meatballs in fine breadcrumbs and baking them in a greased muffin tin, which builds a crust and keeps them plump. A 1,080-vote comment argues the opposite, insisting you should fry rather than bake, and adds two of its own rules: a tablespoon of ricotta per pound of meat, and a mix of veal, pork and beef. Two further high-voted notes defend baking, one on a rack at 400F so the fat drains and they brown all over, another at 375F on convection. The most broadly useful tip (966 votes) is to soak the panko or breadcrumbs in milk first, which prevents them drying the meatballs out and improves binding. For even sizing, pat the mixture into a rectangle and cut squares before rolling, or use a small scoop.

name: Meera Sodha’s Naan
headnote: Sam Sifton introduces this as a recipe the British cookbook author learned from her aunt Harsha and published in Made in India in 2015. The flatbreads come out crackly and blistered outside but tender within, with a slight yogurt tang, made for dragging through curry. He advises setting up an assembly line to roll and pan-cook them, and says two or three attempts will end your naan buying.
comment_digest: Hydration is the theme. The top note (935 votes) recommends mixing everything except the flour first, because the liquid-to-flour ratio needs adjusting by feel rather than by the stated measure, and a 118-vote reply gives the same advice as a fix for a specific cook's problem: withhold a few tablespoons of flour and judge the dough's consistency. A 600-vote comment describes a stand mixer method, wet ingredients with sugar and yeast first using the paddle, dry sprinkled in after, again holding back some flour. A 596-vote note confirms the dough freezes well wrapped as individual balls. For those without a suitable pan, a 152-vote comment bakes them on a pizza stone or sheet tray at about 470F until they puff, then flips them. Yogurt is essential and has no easy substitute.

name: My Favorite Challah
headnote: Joan Nathan opens with the word's origin, the small portion of dough set aside when baking bread as a remembrance of the destruction of the Temple, and traces how it became the sweet, brioche-like braided loaf brought to America from Central and Eastern Europe. Braided loaves are year-round; round ones, often with raisins, belong to Rosh Hashana, Yom Kippur and Sukkot. Her accumulated tips from bakers in the US, Europe and Israel: multiple risings improve the loaf, one slow rise in the refrigerator gives a more brioche-like crumb, and two coats of egg wash produce the gloss.
comment_digest: Two notes matter most. The highest-voted (994) supplies the gram weights the recipe lacks: 3 1/2 teaspoons active dry yeast at 9.9g, 1 tablespoon sugar at 12.6g, 1/2 cup sugar at 100g, 1/2 cup vegetable oil at 120g, 1 tablespoon salt at 17.07g, and 8 to 8 1/2 cups all-purpose flour at 960 to 1020g; a separate 449-vote comment is the request that prompted it, asking the Times to publish weights. The other significant correction (560 votes) states the six-strand braiding instructions are written incorrectly. A 466-vote baker adds a sponge step, using part of the flour and liquid first, for better brioche flavour and texture. A 245-vote note swaps in 1/2 cup plus 1 tablespoon honey for the sugar and steeps a pinch of saffron in boiling water. A 757-vote comment explains the pale bands in the photograph come from oven spring exposing new surface after the wash.
flags: comments report the six-braid instructions are wrong; top comment supplies gram weights useful for the collection

name: Oklahoma Onion Burgers
headnote: J. Kenji Lopez-Alt traces this to Homer Davis and his son Ross at the Hamburger Inn in El Reno, Oklahoma, where it began as a Depression-era way of bulking out a burger cheaply with onion. The patties are smashed under a heap of very thinly shaved onions, and the buns are steamed in the onion vapour rather than toasted. He notes you can move the whole operation outdoors by setting the skillet or griddle over a hot grill, which also keeps the onion smell out of the house.
comment_digest: The comments are unusually consensual: almost nobody argues with the method. A 74-vote note says El Reno has done it this way for eighty years and they know best. The most concrete cooking advice (106 votes) endorses the recipe's own suggestion of putting the cast-iron pan on an outdoor grill to avoid filling the house with onion smoke, and a 58-vote comment recommends a portable induction cooktop for the same reason. A 255-vote commenter whose former partner's grandfather ran an Oklahoma diner reports the family version used diced rather than sliced onion and no cheese. Bun choice gets real attention: Martin's potato rolls (62 votes) for softness without sweetness, or Trader Joe's brioche buns (50) as a sturdier brioche. One note stresses the details that matter: when to salt, and scraping the pan hard so all the browned crust ends up in the burger.

name: One-Pot Spaghetti with Cherry Tomatoes and Kale
headnote: Tejal Rao presents the internet-famous one-pan method, raw pasta simmered together with cherry tomatoes so the starch thickens into its own sauce, in the vegetarian version by British author Anna Jones, adapted from A Modern Way to Cook. The headnote pushes the adaptability: anchovies and a good pinch of red-pepper flakes can go in with the kale, and chopped mint, basil or oregano can be piled on with the cheese at the end.
comment_digest: The big disagreement is whether cooking pasta this way is worth doing at all. A 522-vote comment defends it firmly, arguing the unconventional cooking is the entire point and that making it the normal way produces a different dish; a 382-vote note takes the opposite line, saying conventional pasta cooking is better and that the recipe is fine mainly as a base for whatever greens you have, arugula or Swiss chard included. A 285-vote reply deflates the one-pot claim, pointing out you can boil water in an electric kettle. On seasoning, the most-repeated advice is to be generous: plenty of garlic and red chili flakes (695 votes), with a 312-vote cook sauteing onion and garlic first and adding a splash of wine. A 1,059-vote comment is a joke about pasta purism.

name: Original Plum Torte
headnote: Marian Burros's torte ran in the Times every September from 1983 to 1989, when editors decided to retire it and printed it one last time in larger type with a dotted border for clipping. Readers revolted with a flood of angry letters, one from Tarrytown telling the paper not to be grumpy about summer ending, and the Times has pledged ever since to keep it available each year. The 1983 original used a cup of sugar and the 1989 revision cut it to three-quarters; both are given.
comment_digest: With nearly 4,000 notes the top-voted one (4,606) is a question about the flour: whether "1 cup flour, sifted" means sift then measure or measure then sift. A 4,106-vote reply settles it, explaining that sifted flour means sift first then measure, while flour, sifted means measure first then sift, so this recipe measures a cup and sifts it. The next-highest (4,225) is a much-loved story about baking it to make a house smell good enough to sell. Practical variations are popular: raspberries and blackberries, a basket each, in place of plums, with about a third of a cup of cornmeal added (1,955 votes); slicing the plums and fanning them out rather than using halves, which looks better and distributes fruit more evenly, plus a little lemon (1,397). It is widely reported as a reliable family standby.

name: Panettone
headnote: A panettone from pastry chef Andrea Tortora on Great Italian Chefs, first published in 2016. The site rates it as challenging and gives a 48-hour timeline, warning that the timing must be managed carefully and that patience is the main requirement. It describes panettone as the emblem of an Italian Christmas, complex and aromatic, and notes that special equipment is needed. The page adds, cheerfully, that anyone put off by the difficulty can buy Tortora's own panettone from selected UK shops instead.
comment_digest: NO COMMENTS
flags: non-paywalled site with no comments section and no ratings yet; recipe is a 48-hour project requiring special equipment

name: Zucchini Gratin
headnote: Food Network publishes no headnote for this one. The page credits it to Ina Garten and sources it to her book Barefoot in Paris, listing it as an easy side dish taking about an hour and five minutes and serving six, built on sliced yellow onions and zucchini cooked down with butter.
comment_digest: Food Network sorts reviews by date rather than helpfulness and shows no vote counts, so there is no clear ranking of usefulness. The overall rating is 4.5 across 449 reviews and the tone is mostly positive, with several cooks calling it their favourite zucchini dish and a good way to use up a glut or even leftover sauteed zucchini and onions. Reported variations that worked include chopped garlic scapes and substituting Parmesan for the specified cheese. The recurring criticism is texture and blandness: one reviewer found the zucchini too soft and wanted more spice, and another said the sauce gives it the character of a green bean casserole. Cooking the zucchini less, and seasoning more assertively, are the adjustments those complaints point to.
flags: Food Network page: no headnote, reviews sorted by recency with no helpfulness votes so digest cannot be ranked by consensus
